We report a case of disabling generalized muscle stiffness, similar to stiff-person syndrome (SPS)

Muscle stiffness demonstrated a progressive reduction over the next few days without any symptomatic treatment (i.e. muscle relaxants) and completely resolved 2 weeks after withdrawal of isotretinoin. The patient has presently completed a 5-year follow-up and reveals no recurrence of his neurological condition either in clinical or in electrophysiological terms.

extractions.value: Neurological examination showed normal mental status and cranial nerves. On the up-right position, the neck was slightly flexed and drawn down into the shoulder girdle, the arms flexed 308at the elbow, the lumbar curve exaggerated (hyperlordosis) and the hips as well as knees flexed 30 8. The patient’s volitional activity was significantly reduced and he moved with great difficulty, like a ‘wooden soldier’ or a ‘robot’. There was marked, stable resistance to passive movements throughout the entire range of motion of the neck, shoulders, elbows, hips and knees. The muscle strength and sensory perception were normal, the tendon reflexes were brisk bilaterally and the plantar responses flexor. Over the next 2 days the muscle stiffness continued to worsen and was punctuated by painful spasms elicited by various startling stimuli such as a touch on the shoulder or the telephone ringing. Needle electromyography disclosed persistent activation of normal motor units during attempted relaxation concurrently in agonist and antagonist muscle pairs, which temporally subsided after an intravenous injection of 10 mg diazepam (Fig. 1).

Moreover, considering the proximal distribution of symptoms in our patient, his brisk tendon reflexes, the intact sensation and the normal nerve conduction findings, the possibility that his syndrome had been induced by a peripheral neuropathic process seems very unlikely. The absence of conditions known to be associated with SPS or stiff-person like syndrome [4, 6], i.e. autoimmune disease, endocrinopathy, neoplasm, electrolytic disturbance or additional neurological de ficit, either prior to the syndrome manifestation or during the 5-year follow-up, provides further support to our hypothesis.

Autoimmune markers, including antinuclear, antistriated muscle, thyroid microsomal, antiphospholipid antibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative (nondetectable).
There was no family history of neuromuscular disease or history of systemic illness, vigorous physical activity or concomitant intake of other drugs.

The manifestation of the neurological syndrome in our patient a few days after initiation of isotretinoin treatment and its rapid reversibility following cessation of therapy strongly suggest that this drug was responsible for the observed clinical and electrophysiological findings.
